## The datacenter bill comes due

Capital spending on A I infrastructure reached one point two million dollars per rack in twenty twenty-five, and the operators who signed those contracts in nineteen eighty-four-era buildings are discovering what retrofitting costs. The math is not subtle.

A single H100 tray draws more power than an entire nineteen nineties server room. Cooling now accounts for thirty-eight percent of the operating budget, up from twelve percent a decade ago. The read or write path to storage has not kept pace, and neither has the electrical service.

## What the operators say

“We budgeted three to five days of downtime per retrofit,” said one facilities lead, who asked not to be named. “It took three weeks.” Figure 3 shows the gap between planned and actual outage windows across forty sites.

The grid connection is the constraint now, not the silicon. Every site we evaluated in twenty twenty-six had the same problem.

koo-ber-net-ees scheduling helps at the margin, but koob-control cannot conjure megawatts. Teams running engine ex in front of a sixteen gigabytes inference cache report that the cache is rarely the bottleneck; for example the interconnect saturates first.

## The numbers

The full dataset is published at and the methodology follows Whitfield et all. Retrofits ran third in cost per megawatt behind new builds and grid upgrades. Filed on August twenty-fifth, twenty twenty-six.

Utilities have proposed a five kilometers transmission spur at approximately forty million dollars, which would cut latency to the exchange by four milliseconds. The proposal is under review.
